chapters.title: Chapter 2: Market Impact and Liquidity: Why Big Money Moves Prices

lessons.title: Market Impact 101: The Square-Root Law of Price Impact

children.text: The last lesson showed market impact mechanically, one order walking through five levels of a book. This lesson turns that mechanical picture into a model you can actually use for planning, the square-root law of market impact, one of the most widely relied-upon rules of thumb on any trading desk that has to think about size.
Two Kinds of Market Impact: Temporary and Permanent

markDefs.definition: The portion of price impact caused mechanically by depleting available liquidity while you trade, which tends to fade and let the price revert partway once your trading pressure stops.
The portion of price impact that does not revert, because your trading revealed information the market has now incorporated into the price going forward.

children.text: Not all impact is the same kind of cost.
is the book-walking effect from the last lesson, it fades once you stop trading.

does not fade, because your trading pattern told the market something, and the price stays at its new level. This distinction connects directly to crowding from Chapter 1: a signal so public that others can detect and follow your trading tends to carry a much larger permanent component.

children.text: The Square-Root Law: An Empirical Regularity

Transaction cost analysis on trading desks worldwide, including many Indian prop and quant desks, has repeatedly found the same empirical pattern: total market impact cost scales roughly with the square root of order size relative to average daily volume, not linearly with order size. This is an observed regularity, refined and recalibrated across markets and time periods, not a law of physics, but it is stable enough to be the default starting model almost everywhere.

body.caption: I(Q) is impact cost as a fraction of price. sigma is the stock's daily volatility. Q is order size and ADV is average daily volume, in the same units (shares or rupee value). Y is an empirical calibration constant, commonly between 0.5 and 1 for large and mid-cap equities.

children.text: Worked example: a stock has daily volatility of 2 percent and average daily volume of Rs 10 crore. You want to trade Rs 2.5 crore, a participation ratio of 25 percent. Using a calibration constant Y of 0.75, the square root of 0.25 is 0.5, so impact cost is 0.75 times 2 percent times 0.5, which comes out to 0.75 percent of trade value.

stats.label: Participation ratio (Q / ADV)
stats.context: Rs 2.5 crore order against Rs 10 crore ADV

children.text: A square-root relationship is concave: cost keeps rising as order size grows, but each additional rupee of size adds a little less cost than the rupee before it. Double your order size and impact cost rises by roughly 41 percent, not 100 percent, because a patient execution can spread the order across time and across willing counterparties rather than dumping it all at once. That is genuinely useful, but do not mistake it for good news. Cost is still rising continuously with size, there is no size at which it plateaus for free, and the constant Y itself tends to get worse, not better, once participation ratios climb past what a market can comfortably absorb.

body.title: Illustrative Impact Cost vs Participation Ratio

body.text: Because impact cost scales with the square root of participation, the relationship flips instructively once you solve for capacity instead of cost: if you double how much impact cost you are willing to tolerate, you roughly quadruple how much capital you can deploy, since capacity is proportional to the square of your cost budget, not simply proportional to it. Chapter 4 builds directly on this relationship to estimate a strategy's practical capacity.

body.title: Apply the Square-Root Law
body.prompt: A stock has daily volatility of 1.5%. Average daily volume is Rs 20 crore. You want to trade Rs 5 crore, a participation ratio of 25%. Using the square-root model with a calibration constant Y of 0.8, what is the estimated impact cost, as a percentage of trade value? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: The square root of 5/20 = 0.25 is 0.5. Impact cost = 0.8 x 1.5% x 0.5 = 0.006, or 0.6% of trade value.

body.text: Market impact cost grows with the square root of order size relative to liquidity, not one-for-one with size. It is gentler than a naive linear guess would suggest, but it never stops rising, and that single relationship is the mathematical seed of every capacity estimate in this course.

points: Market impact splits into temporary impact, which fades once trading stops, and permanent impact, which persists because trading revealed information, closely tied to crowding.

The square-root law states that impact cost scales roughly with the square root of order size relative to average daily volume, an empirical regularity used across global trading desks rather than a fixed physical law.
Because the relationship is concave, doubling order size raises impact cost by about 41%, not 100%, though total cost keeps rising continuously with size.

Since cost scales with the square root of size, capacity scales with the square of your acceptable cost budget, a relationship Chapter 4 uses directly to estimate how much capital a strategy can actually absorb.
